passage: On Lalit's first morning as the new teacher at the village middle school, the six staff sat on the veranda mat with steel cups of tea. Ritu, the headmistress, handed Lalit a cup and a piece of jaggery. “On a newcomer's first Monday, everyone says one thing they like about this school,” she said. The old maths teacher grinned and said, “The breeze.” The clerk said, “The children's singing.” The science teacher said nothing and only sipped. Lalit's shoulders had been tight since the bus ride. Ritu added, “It's not a test. We just want you to know how we start. Tomorrow you needn't bring anything.” Lalit smiled and said, “The bell that rings a little late,” and everybody laughed.

qa.q: What did Ritu hand to Lalit with the cup of tea?
qa.a: Ritu handed Lalit a piece of jaggery with the cup of tea.

qa.q: What might Lalit have been feeling on the bus ride and at the start of the morning?
qa.a: Lalit was probably nervous about being the newcomer, since Lalit's shoulders had been tight since the bus ride.

qa.q: What did Ritu do that helped Lalit feel included and not tested?
qa.a: Ritu explained the small ritual and said plainly that it was not a test and that nothing needed to be brought, so the newcomer could join in easily.

qa.q: What might the science teacher, who said nothing and only sipped, have been thinking?
qa.a: The science teacher may have been shy or unsure what to say, and may still have been glad to sit with the group. 🙂

grounding: A wise team welcomes a newcomer with a simple, warm ritual and explains its meaning so the newcomer feels included and not tested.

passage: On Wanjiru's first Friday in the Toronto lab, at four o'clock everybody drifted toward the meeting table. A cake sat in the middle. Xin, the senior scientist, said, “The new person picks next week's cake, and everyone shares one good thing from the week. You're allowed to pass.” A postdoc, Dan, said his experiment finally ran. Another said her sister had a baby. One student stared at his plate. When it came to Wanjiru, she hesitated, then said, “I found the coffee machine.” Everyone laughed. Xin leaned over. “We started this so new people wouldn't have to guess how things work here. Next Friday it's yours to choose.” Wanjiru relaxed and asked what flavours people liked.

qa.q: What did the new person get to pick for next week?
qa.a: The new person picks next week's cake.

qa.q: What was Wanjiru feeling when Wanjiru hesitated before speaking?
qa.a: Wanjiru was probably a little nervous and unsure what was expected, since Wanjiru was new and the group all looked toward her.

qa.q: What did Xin say that made the ritual welcoming?
qa.a: Xin explained that the ritual was started so new people would not have to guess how things work, and said passing was allowed.

qa.q: What might the student who stared at his plate have been feeling?
qa.a: The student may have felt shy about sharing, which the rule that anyone can pass could ease.

grounding: A wise team welcomes a newcomer with a simple ritual, explaining that it exists so newcomers do not have to guess, so the newcomer feels included.

passage: On Jaya's first morning on the children's ward, the night staff were leaving and the day staff crowded into the tiny pantry. Sudha, the senior nurse, handed Jaya a steel tumbler of tea and said, 'Ward 3 tradition. Five minutes. Everyone says one thing they're worried about today and one thing they're looking forward to. No one's graded.' Jaya's throat went tight; she hated speaking first in new places. Sudha went first: 'Worried about bed 6's fever. Looking forward to Rahim going home.' The others followed. When Jaya's turn came, she said, 'Worried I'll get lost. Looking forward to learning names.' Everyone laughed kindly, and a porter drew her a map on a napkin. Later Sudha walked her through the other unwritten rules: who to call at night, where the good trolley is kept.

qa.q: What did Sudha hand Jaya?
qa.a: A steel tumbler of tea.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel when the ritual was explained?
qa.a: Her throat went tight; she felt nervous, because she hated speaking first in new places.

qa.q: What made Sudha's welcome inclusive rather than a test?
qa.a: She explained the ritual's meaning, said no one was graded, went first herself, and later explained the unwritten rules.

qa.q: How might the porter feel drawing Jaya a map?
qa.a: The porter likely felt glad to help and part of the welcome, turning a newcomer's small worry into a shared moment.

grounding: A ward team welcomes a new nurse with a simple ritual, explains its meaning and the unwritten habits, so she feels included.

passage:
Dear Kiran didi,
I wanted to thank you properly for Saturday. When I walked into your parents' house for my first Pongal as Arun's wife, I was terrified of doing something wrong. Then you took me aside before the pot boiled and explained everything: why we shout 'Pongalo Pongal' when the milk spills over, why the first spoonful goes to the cow, why Amma puts sugarcane by the door. You said, 'Nobody's testing you. We just want you in it.'
When the milk rose, your little cousins pulled me to the front and we all shouted together. Amma handed me the first plate for the cow.
I felt like part of the family, not a guest.
With love,
Damini

qa.q: When does the family shout 'Pongalo Pongal'?
qa.a: When the milk spills over.

qa.q: How did Damini feel walking in for the first Pongal?
qa.a: Damini felt terrified of doing something wrong in the new family.

qa.q: What did Kiran do that made the ritual welcoming?
qa.a: She explained each custom and its meaning beforehand and said nobody was testing Damini, so Damini could join without fear.

qa.q: What might Amma have meant by handing Damini the first plate for the cow?
qa.a: Amma was likely showing acceptance, giving the newcomer an important part of the ritual to say she belongs.

grounding: A family welcomes a new member into a festival ritual by explaining its meaning, so she feels included rather than tested.

passage: Leela, you want to know about our team's first-Friday plant? I'm Gargi, I lead a small support team at an insurance office, and I used to hate how new people were just thrown in. So now, on a new person's first Friday, the whole team buys a small potted plant, and everyone writes one tip on a card: where the good stapler is, which manager hates emojis in emails, how to escape the long meetings. We sit around the plant and explain each card. Last month a new joiner, Ibrahim, told us he'd been scared we'd test him with trick questions. By the end he was laughing and writing his own card for the next person. The plant's on his desk now. Honestly, that's the whole culture.

qa.q: What does the team buy on a new person's first Friday?
qa.a: A small potted plant.

qa.q: How did Ibrahim feel before the first-Friday plant?
qa.a: He was scared the team would test him with trick questions.

qa.q: Why do the tip cards work so well?
qa.a: They make the unwritten habits clear, like where the stapler is or which manager hates emojis, so the newcomer feels included, not tested.

qa.q: What might it mean for Ibrahim to write his own card for the next person?
qa.a: It shows he now feels part of the team and wants to pass the welcome on.

grounding: A team welcomes newcomers with a simple ritual that explains the unwritten habits, so they feel included.

passage: I've sat by the window at our design studio for three years, so I saw Kamal's first morning. He came in at 9:05, holding his laptop bag like a shield. Nandini, our lead, didn't hand him a login sheet first. She walked him to the plant by the pantry. "Everyone who joins waters this on day one," she said. "It was Jojo's, our first designer. It means you're one of the people who keep things alive here." Kamal laughed nervously, but he watered it. Then she told him the other unwritten stuff: nobody expects replies after seven, Friday lunch is together, and it's fine to say "I don't know" in reviews. I watched his shoulders drop. By lunch he was arguing about pickle with Harpreet as if he'd been here for years.

qa.q: What does everyone who joins do on day one?
qa.a: Everyone who joins waters the plant by the pantry on day one.

qa.q: How can you tell Kamal went from nervous to at ease?
qa.a: He held his bag like a shield and laughed nervously, then his shoulders dropped and by lunch he was arguing about pickle, so he felt relaxed and accepted.

qa.q: Why did Nandini explain the unwritten habits on the first day?
qa.a: Spelling out things like no replies after seven and saying "I don't know" in reviews meant Kamal didn't have to guess or feel tested.

qa.q: How might Harpreet experience the new colleague by lunch?
qa.a: Harpreet likely finds Kamal easy to talk to already, since the warm welcome helped him settle into the team.

grounding: The narrator watches a team lead welcome a newcomer with a simple ritual and explain the unwritten habits so he feels included.
